name: Pancreatic panniculitis
aliases: subcutaneous fat necrosis of pancreatic disease

clinicalPearls: Presents as tender, erythematous to violaceous subcutaneous nodules, classically on the lower legs but also thighs, buttocks and trunk
Nodules may soften, ulcerate and discharge an oily brown viscous material as liquefied fat is released
It signals underlying pancreatic disease, most often acute or chronic pancreatitis but also pancreatic carcinoma (especially acinar cell type)
Skin lesions can precede recognition of the pancreatic disorder, so unexplained leg nodules warrant pancreatic evaluation
The triad of panniculitis, polyarthritis and eosinophilia (PPP syndrome) carries a worse prognosis
Biopsy shows a lobular panniculitis with pathognomonic anucleate 'ghost' adipocytes and basophilic saponification of fat by calcium salts
Treatment is directed at the underlying pancreatic disease; the skin improves as the pancreatic process is controlled
reference.pathophysiology: Pancreatic panniculitis results from release of pancreatic enzymes, principally lipase, amylase and trypsin, into the circulation during pancreatic inflammation or from an enzyme-secreting tumour. These enzymes reach the subcutaneous fat and hydrolyse triglycerides, liberating free fatty acids that combine with calcium to form insoluble soaps (saponification). This enzymatic fat necrosis destroys adipocytes, leaving characteristic anucleate ghost cells with thick shadowy walls and basophilic granular calcium deposits, surrounded by a mixed inflammatory infiltrate within the fat lobules.
additionalDifferentials: Subcutaneous fat necrosis of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Deep incisional biopsy of a fresh nodule including subcutaneous fat
Cross-sectional pancreatic imaging (CT or MRI) to identify pancreatitis or tumour
Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia
Tumour markers and further evaluation if pancreatic carcinoma is suspected
redFlags: Panniculitis with polyarthritis and eosinophilia (PPP syndrome), which is associated with high mortality
Nodules arising without an obvious cause, raising suspicion of occult pancreatic carcinoma
Features of severe acute pancreatitis with systemic compromise
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on the underlying pancreatic disease: lesions accompanying self-limiting pancreatitis resolve as the pancreas recovers, whereas panniculitis linked to pancreatic carcinoma or the PPP syndrome carries a poor prognosis. Skin nodules often heal with atrophic hyperpigmented scars.
pitfalls: Dismissing recurrent leg nodules as ordinary erythema nodosum and missing the pancreatic cause
Failing to search for an occult pancreatic tumour when pancreatitis is absent
Sampling too superficially to demonstrate the diagnostic saponified ghost adipocytes
Overlooking accompanying arthritis and eosinophilia that portend a worse course
